description: Team of six (devs, designers, entrepreneur) building Water Waltz: a web app using NISAR L-band radar to map water appearing or disappearing, even under clouds and vegetation, and compare it with the normal for each season. Built for civil defense, water managers and communities. Join if you love turning radar data into clear visuals. Looking for: SAR/remote sensing, hydrology, Python/HDF5, data visualization, storytelling.
summary:
Water Waltz is a web app that uses NASA NISAR L-band radar (L2 GCOV) to show where water was observed over time in the Taquari Valley (RS, Brazil), and lets residents check their own location.

In recent floods, many people were affected without water at their door because the road or bridge to their town was cut. A resident can save their home and see whether radar detected water there in the latest image, in how many past images, how far the nearest water was, and whether access may be cut: “affected without being flooded.” We combine NISAR water detection with OpenStreetMap roads and IBGE localities for context.

For the “Dancing with the SARs” challenge, we process a time series of NISAR acquisitions (21 images since June 2026, on two orbits repeating every 12 days) and make radar data understandable to non-experts through a globe, regional map, and timeline.

It matters because radar sees through clouds and at night, and flood impact depends on access as well as inundation. Water Waltz is a candidate indicator that shows only what the radar observed, with documented limits. It is not a forecast or a validated flood map.
details:
What it does and how it works

Water Waltz turns NISAR radar images into a simple answer for residents: “Is my area affected?” A person saves their home location and sees whether radar observed water there in the latest image, in how many of the past images, how far the nearest water was, and whether access may be cut (“affected without being flooded”).

The pipeline works in three stages:

  1. Pipeline (Python): we searched NASA’s catalogue and found 21 NISAR L2 GCOV images since June 2026 covering the Taquari Valley, on two orbits that repeat every 12 days. Scripts run once on our computers and apply a simple, documented threshold to detect smooth surfaces that look dark to radar (candidate water). We cross this with OpenStreetMap main roads (motorway to tertiary) and IBGE municipal seats to estimate access. The output is images and numbers in data/demo/.
  2. Backend (FastAPI): serves the processed files, with no live processing.
  3. Frontend (Next.js, JavaScript): a globe, a regional map, a timeline of observations, and the “Is my area affected?” tool, deployed on Vercel.

Benefits and intended impact

Flood response often focuses on who is under water. In the Taquari Valley, many people were isolated because roads or bridges were cut. Water Waltz shows that second kind of impact and makes radar data, which sees through clouds and at night, understandable to non-experts. Our intended impact is to help residents understand their situation and to point toward a future detailed view for Civil Defence.

Tools and technologies

  • NASA NISAR L2 GCOV (the only source of candidate water)
  • Python for data processing; FastAPI and pytest for the backend
  • Next.js and React for the frontend; Vercel for deployment
  • OpenStreetMap (tiles and roads, ODbL) and IBGE Base de Localidades 2022 for context
  • GitHub with CI running npm audit on every pull request
  • AI coding tools for parts of the code, with all code reviewed and tested by the team

Creativity

The name and idea reframe a radar dance (“Dancing with the SARs”) as a story told from a resident’s doorstep: not “where is the flood” but “can I get out, and can help get in.” Combining radar water observations with road access is the core creative step.

Factors we considered

  • Honesty about limits: smooth surfaces and shadows also look dark; wind, cities, and flooded vegetation can hide water; not seeing water does not prove there was no flood. The app is labeled a candidate indicator, not a validated flood map, and not for evacuation or route decisions.
  • No forecasting: it only shows what the radar observed, and NISAR revisits every 12 days.
  • Licensing and attribution: OSM attribution is always visible, and the road file stays under ODbL while the code is MIT.
  • Security and reliability: response headers set in next.config.mjs, patched dependencies, and a validation step that refuses test data before publishing.
  • Future work: AI water classification validated against independent NASA data, automatic updates from NISAR and Sentinel-1, hydrological forecasts, and alerts for authorities.
